description: We are a team of engineering and technology students from Unicamp and UFF, Brazil, passionate about innovation, science, and solving real-world challenges! 🚀 We bring experience in programming, robotics, AI, automation, and engineering. Our goal is to build creative, impactful solutions while learning and collaborating. We're looking for curious, motivated teammates with skills in coding, data science, design, aerospace, or storytelling. Let's create something extraordinary together! 🌎
summary: With weather growing less predictable, farmers face risks that reach beyond their fields: a lost harvest threatens family income, local markets and food security. NATIVA helps Brazilian farmers decide what to plant after soybean in the off-season (safrinha), with clear, science-based guidance. The farmer draws a field on the map and tells us the current rotation. NATIVA reads 35 years of NASA POWER climate, NASADEM terrain, HLS satellite imagery, soil maps and municipal yields for that field. It removes the options that the law or the planting calendar rules out, then compares up to 22 rotations on income, soil, water, pests and climate risk. Income is estimated as municipal yield × market price − CONAB production cost. Every option comes with an explanation card: why it ranks where it does, the evidence, the benefits, the data gaps and the risks, including how much income it gives up against the best-earning option. The engine is transparent rules and scores, with no black-box model. Tested on 16 past seasons it had never seen, its income decision gained +1.54 soybean bags/ha/yr across Paraná, in every region of the state, and its climate risk agreed with the official zoning (ZARC) 90 % of the time. NATIVA covers all 399 municipalities of Paraná, helping farmers adapt to climate uncertainty while protecting their livelihoods and communities.
details:
1. The challenge: one decision, one season, no second chance

In Western Paraná, almost every field grows soybean in summer. The real decision comes in February, when the soybean is harvested: what goes in next? Off-season corn pays well but freezes in cold years. A cover crop protects the soil but earns little. Wheat, beans, sorghum and oats each bring different risks. Farmers make this call once a year, with their own money, after seasons like the 2021/22 drought (about 75% soybean loss in the Toledo region) and the 2021 frost, the worst off-season corn loss in the state's history.

NASA has decades of climate, terrain and satellite data that bear on this decision. Turning them into an answer for one specific field is the hard part, and that is the challenge NATIVA takes on.

2. Our solution: NATIVA

NATIVA is a crop-rotation decision-support tool. It does not answer "what grows here?". It answers "of the rotations I can legally and practically do on this field, which one fits my priorities, what will it earn, and what could go wrong?"

The farmer stays in control. The farmer's current rotation is always part of the comparison, and they can set how much income, soil, water, pests and risk matter to them. They can also replace our estimates with their own numbers: soil analysis, yields, prices, costs, irrigation, crops they cannot sell, and crops they do not want to grow.

3. How it works

Step 1 — The field. The farmer draws the field boundary on a map or drops a point. Our demo field (72638, ~104 ha in Toledo, PR) was outlined with Fields of the World. It is most likely the micro-watershed studied by Embrapa Soja and Itaipu, so we can check the tool against published field facts.

Step 2 — Diagnosis. For that field, NATIVA puts together:

  • Climate (NASA POWER, daily since 1991): frost in the flowering and grain-filling phase, water deficit and reference evapotranspiration, all computed for the farmer's sowing date;
  • Terrain (NASADEM, 30 m): elevation and slope;
  • Observed rotation (NASA HLS, Landsat + Sentinel-2, 30 m NDVI): the annual land-use map (MapBiomas) labels most fields simply as "soybean". The HLS time series shows the second crop the farmer actually grew;
  • Soil (SoilGrids): clay, sand, organic carbon, pH and water-holding capacity. A farmer's soil analysis replaces them;
  • Land-use history (MapBiomas 2019–2024) and municipal yields (IBGE PAM).

Step 3 — Hard rules first. Before any scoring, NATIVA removes the rotations that are not allowed and says why:

  • soybean during the soybean-free period, or soybean after soybean (Portaria SDA/MAPA 1.579/2026, by ADAPAR region);
  • sowing windows (ZARC/IDR-PR references);
  • a second crop that cannot follow the summer harvest;
  • the farmer's own restrictions.

ZARC does not ban crops, but it conditions rural credit and insurance, so NATIVA shows a ZARC warning on the option's card.

Step 4 — Five criteria, one transparent score. Each remaining rotation gets five scores from 0 to 1:

  • Income: margin compared with plain soybean in the municipality, from the IBGE PAM yield trend × SEAB/DERAL prices − CONAB costs;
  • Soil: straw, ground cover and nitrogen, from the agronomic catalog and the soil texture;
  • Water: water stress in the second crop, from an FAO-56 daily water balance (POWER ET0 + soil water capacity);
  • Pests: pest and disease pressure, e.g., corn on corn, from catalog rules;
  • Climate risk: probability of frost or water deficit for the chosen sowing date, from NASA POWER since 1991.

The final score is a weighted average. Income has the highest default weight (5, the others 3), and the farmer can change any weight from 0 to 10. NATIVA does not hide the trade-off between profit and soil health. When an option ranks above a higher-earning one because of soil or pest benefits, its card says how many reais per hectare per year it gives up.

Step 5 — Explained recommendations. Every ranked option has a card with:

  • why it ranks where it does;
  • the evidence (e.g., "frost in the critical phase in X% of years, NASA POWER");
  • the benefits, the data gaps and the risks.

Each option also carries its uncertainty: the range of income and score across the last five seasons and how often it would have ranked first. When the top options are within 0.02 points, NATIVA calls it a technical tie and leaves the choice to the farmer's priorities. The cards are built directly from the computed numbers; no language model writes them.

Example (field 72638, default weights):

  • 1st — Soybean → off-season corn + brachiaria: score 0.798, estimated margin R$ 2,994/ha;
  • 2nd — Soybean → millet / crotalaria (cover): score 0.756, estimated margin R$ 1,103/ha;
  • 3rd — Soybean → off-season corn (current rotation): score 0.755, estimated margin R$ 2,954/ha.

Corn + brachiaria keeps almost all the income of the current rotation and adds soil cover. The cover crop is second on soil and pests, and its card states the income it costs.

4. Does it work? Validation

We ran the engine on 16 past seasons it had never seen and compared its choice with what the harvest actually paid. The numbers:

  • +1.26 soybean bags/ha/yr from the income decision in Western Paraná, better in 13 of 16 seasons. Across all of Paraná (288 municipalities), the gain is +1.54 bags/ha/yr, in every region of the state.
  • 82% hit rate on the most profitable option, up from 72%, with a 19% smaller margin error.
  • 90% agreement with ZARC, Brazil's official climate-risk zoning: the engine's off-season corn risk lands within one ZARC class (κ = 0.63).
  • 24% predicted loss on off-season corn, against 23% observed in 1,143 municipality-seasons (2003–2025).

On a real field (72638, Toledo): corn + brachiaria comes first (score 0.799). Replayed over the last 5 seasons, its score stays between 0.68 and 0.82, and it is first in 4 of them.

The NASA inputs are checked on the ground too: POWER minimum temperature correlates at 0.94 with INMET stations, and HLS NDVI on 335 fields confirms the soybean → off-season corn pattern in 93% of them.

Sources: NASA POWER and HLS, IBGE PAM, CONAB, SEAB/DERAL, ZARC/MAPA · 50 municipalities in Western Paraná, seasons 2010–2025.

5. Technology

  • Engine and API: Python 3.12 and FastAPI. The API is stateless, every result can be reproduced from its inputs, and responses come in Portuguese or English.
  • Frontend: React + Vite + TypeScript, with a map for drawing the field.
  • Data pipeline: heavy NASA datasets (POWER, NASADEM, HLS) are pre-processed into Parquet/GeoTIFF; SoilGrids is queried live when needed.
  • Current-conditions panel: ENSO, MJO (NOAA), current SMAP soil moisture and pest alerts are shown for context. They do not change the score.
  • Deployment: the frontend is on Vercel, and the API runs in Docker on an Azure VM with HTTPS.
  • Quality: pytest suite, invariant and golden tests, ruff.
  • Generative AI tools helped with coding, debugging, documentation and research. The recommendation engine itself uses no AI model: it is explicit rules and formulas.

6. What makes NATIVA different

  • Field level, Brazil first. Most tools stop at the municipality or the region. NATIVA works on the field the farmer draws, on Brazil's real crop system, with Brazil's real legal calendar.
  • NASA data change the answer. The same calculation gives different recommendations on different farms: frequent frost in one municipality pushes off-season corn down; in a warmer one, corn goes up.
  • Satellite sees what maps miss. HLS reveals the second crop that the annual land-use maps miss.
  • Honest about trade-offs and uncertainty. NATIVA states the income cost of soil-friendly choices, the range across past seasons, technical ties and data gaps, and it never presents an estimate as a promise.
  • Validated against reality, not just demonstrated.

7. Limitations (stated openly)

  • Coverage is the state of Paraná (399 municipalities); areas outside it are refused rather than guessed. Sowing windows and market texts are calibrated for Western Paraná.
  • The NASA POWER climate cell is about 50 km, so local microclimates are not represented.
  • Prices and costs are state-level references (SEAB/DERAL, CONAB). Farm margins differ, and farmers can enter their own numbers.
  • Some agronomic coefficients (soil benefit, pest break) are catalog estimates, labelled as such in every response.
  • NATIVA does not replace an agronomist or the official ZARC.

8. What's next

  • Expand to other Brazilian states. MapBiomas and NASADEM already cover Brazil. Each new state needs the climate pipeline run on its grid and its legal calendar added.
  • Use current conditions in the score: SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall for the current season.
  • Blind ranking by agronomists (Embrapa, IDR-PR, cooperatives) as the next validation layer.
  • Multi-year rotation plans and farm-specific cost sheets.

9. Our vision

A farmer in Paraná should not need to be a climate scientist, a remote-sensing analyst or an economist to use what NASA observes from space. NATIVA turns those observations into one clear comparison: what each option earns, what it does for the soil, and what could go wrong, with the reasons laid out. Better decisions before planting.
